newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia hits Thai aid critics as cheap, populist.
newsitem.headline: Australia hits Thai aid critics as cheap, populist.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday defended Canberra's US$1 billion contribution to an international financial bail-out of Thailand, calling critics who include controversial politician Pauline Hanson cheap and populist.

Australian support for the US$16 billion International Monetary Fund-brokered rescue package helped secure economic stability in a region vital to Australian trade, Howard said in a speech to political supporters.

"I invite them (critics) to contemplate just for a moment what a poor participant in the Asia-Pacific region Australia would have looked if Japan was in, China was in, Hong Kong was in, Malaysia was in, Indonesia was in, the Philippines was in, but no Australia wasn't," Howard said.

Hanson, who sparked a divisive national race row last year, has joined some commentators and community groups in criticising the Australian contribution, saying the money could be better spent tackling the country's chronic unemployment problem.

Australia on Monday joined the international effort to help Bangkok shore up its currency and weather a financial crisis that has seen scores of finance companies close and forced economic reforms on the Thai government.
Japan and the International Monetary Fund have led the rescue package, with loans of US$4 billion each. Other regional governments have joined in to help protect regional economic stability.
Australia's Labor opposition has fully supported the Howard government's contribution, despite vocal but limited Australian opposition to the move.
Howard said the loan, provided through a currency swap between the two countries' central banks, was also important to Canberra's efforts to forge a strong role for Australia in the region.

"If Australia did not participate in that we would for years into the future have been perceived as people who were just fair weather friends and people who were not prepared to make a contribution to the stability of the economies in the region," he said.
Hanson has struck a chord with voters with her outspoken policies, including opposition to immigration, foreign aid, foreign investment and welfare for native Aborigines.
